subcomponents.title: Uses scene-kit APIs without bypassing or duplicating them

SampleScene.tsx builds the scene from the kit's SceneLayer, Appear, Box, Arrow, SymbolChip, Label, Emphasis and Frame, and takes the kit's SceneProps. The demo has no navigation, stage, scaling or morph code of its own. The kit supplies the mode and nav hook, the Stage fit-scale, sceneKey grouping and the layoutId morphing.
evidence: Talk.tsx: `<Presentation steps={STEPS} title={TITLE} initialMode="browse" />`, imported from presentation-kit/index.ts.
SampleScene.tsx imports Appear, Arrow, Box, Emphasis, Frame, Label, SceneLayer, SymbolChip and SceneProps from the kit. Each RENDER entry uses one of these primitives.
Presentation.tsx calls usePresentationNav, renders Header, Toc, Stage and Footer, and passes `step.Scene` through Stage.
Stage.tsx wraps the Scene in LayoutGroup and AnimatePresence, keyed by `sceneKey(step)`, and passes `payload` and `stepIndex`.

subcomponents.title: Uses stable identities and appropriate grouped-scene architecture

criteria.rationale: Grouping: all nine step modules set `Scene: SampleScene` and `groupKey: 'how-to'`. Stage.tsx keys the motion.div by `sceneKey(step)`. For a step with a groupKey, sceneKey returns `group:<groupKey>:<sceneId>`, so adjacent steps share one key and the same mounted SampleScene instance. Only `payload.step` changes. Identity: SampleScene.tsx renders each entity from the presentation-owned ENTITY_IDS list in entities.ts. Entities are filtered by APPEARS_AT through entitiesAt(payload.step). Each RENDER entry passes a fixed id to a kit node as `id`. The id is a string literal that matches its RENDER key, not an ENTITY.x member. The node consumers (Box, Label, SymbolChip, Emphasis, Frame via morphProps, and Arrow directly) turn that id into `layoutId`. The Appear wrapper is keyed by id, so persisting entities stay mounted and animate in place. groupKey preserves the scene mount; the layoutId values preserve entity identity.
evidence: steps/step-1.tsx through steps/step-9.tsx each have `Scene: SampleScene`, `groupKey: 'how-to'` and `payload: { step: N }` for N = 1 to 9.
Stage.tsx: `<motion.div key={sceneKey(step)}>` containing `<Scene payload={...} stepIndex={...} />`, inside LayoutGroup.
sceneKey.ts: with a groupKey it returns `group:${step.groupKey}:${id}`, where id is a per-Scene-object counter.

nodes/props.ts `morphProps` sets `layoutId: id` and `layout: true`. Box, Label, SymbolChip, Emphasis and Frame spread it. Arrow.tsx sets `layoutId={id}`.
steps/index.ts lists step1 to step9 in STEPS.

subcomponents.title: Maintains clear boundaries and scope discipline

criteria.rationale: The responsibilities are separate. Registry (presentations/index.ts) maps slug to a lazy Talk. Talk.tsx wires Presentation, STEPS and the CSS. entities.ts holds the data. SampleScene.tsx does the rendering. Each step module holds only its content and payload. how-to.css does the styling. The required title input is consumed. Talk passes TITLE to Presentation `title`, and Presentation uses it for `aria-label` and `data-presentation-name`. The kit then renders per-step titles in Header and Footer. The shared kit inputs the demo uses are consumed: `steps`, `title`, `initialMode`, `payload`, `stepIndex`, and the node `id`, `className`, `style` and `data-*` props. One minor point is that `newcomersAt` and `SAMPLE_STEP_COUNT` in entities.ts are exported but not imported anywhere in src or tests. They are demo-local helpers, not a public API input or a shared constant the demo is meant to consume. They don't blur any boundary, so I did not treat them as a failed contract.

Stage renders the canvas at fixed width and height with transform: translate(-50%, -50%) scale(${scale}) inside an overflow-hidden stage. The layoutKey is the TOC visibility flag.

criteria.rationale: The sample presentation owns one stylesheet, how-to.css, which Talk.tsx imports. Talk.tsx wraps the deck in the root class `how-to`. Every rule in how-to.css that targets a kit hook or a generic element sits under `.how-to`. That covers the root, header, title, marker, mode toggle, prev/next buttons, footer, caption, dots, the `[data-presentation-attribution]` hook, the TOC entries, and every rule inside the @media (max-width: 640px) block. Kit hooks used inside the scene are scoped under `.how-to-scene`, the class the presentation puts on its own SceneLayer. Every other selector (.how-to-actor, .how-to-card[data-kind='ghost'], .how-to-arrow path, .how-to-frame-label and so on) is a class namespaced to this presentation. Those classes are its own hooks: only this presentation applies them, in SampleScene.tsx, so the rules cannot match elements in another presentation after client-side navigation. The materialized template presentation.css follows the same pattern. Its kit-hook rules sit under `.__CLASS__`, its other selectors are `.__CLASS__-box` and `.__CLASS__-arrow`, and new-presentation.mjs replaces `__CLASS__` with the slug. Judge C failed the criterion because .how-to-actor, .how-to-card[data-kind='ghost'] and .how-to-arrow path have no `.how-to` ancestor. That reason does not decide the requirement. The requirement allows scoping under the presentation's own root class or hook, and these selectors target the presentation's own namespaced hook classes, which it alone renders. They are not unscoped rules that could leak to other presentations, which is the defect the criterion names. Judges A and B are borne out by the material, so I rule pass.

votes.rationale: Talk.tsx hands the step list and title to the kit's Presentation. SampleScene.tsx builds the scene from the kit's SceneLayer, Appear, Box, Arrow, SymbolChip, Label, Emphasis and Frame, and takes the kit's SceneProps. The demo has no navigation, stage, scaling or morph code of its own. The kit supplies the mode and nav hook, the Stage fit-scale, sceneKey grouping and the layoutId morphing.
evidence: Talk.tsx: `<Presentation steps={STEPS} title={TITLE} initialMode="browse" />`, imported from presentation-kit/index.ts.
SampleScene.tsx imports Appear, Arrow, Box, Emphasis, Frame, Label, SceneLayer, SymbolChip and SceneProps from the kit. Each RENDER entry uses one of these primitives.
Presentation.tsx calls usePresentationNav, renders Header, Toc, Stage and Footer, and passes `step.Scene` through Stage.
Stage.tsx wraps the Scene in LayoutGroup and AnimatePresence, keyed by `sceneKey(step)`, and passes `payload` and `stepIndex`.
nodes/props.ts `morphProps(id)` sets `layout: true` and `layoutId: id`. Box, Label, SymbolChip, Emphasis and Frame spread it; Arrow sets `layoutId={id}` directly.

votes.rationale: Talk.tsx hands the step array to the kit's Presentation, and the shared SampleScene builds the scene from kit primitives. It does not reimplement navigation, staging, or morphing. Talk.tsx imports Presentation from the kit index and renders `<Presentation steps={STEPS} title={TITLE} initialMode="browse" />`. Navigation, chrome, and Stage mounting stay inside the kit: Presentation calls usePresentationNav and renders Header, Toc, Stage, and Footer. SampleScene takes `SceneProps<SamplePayload>`. votes.rationale: The port is reserved ephemerally and --strictPort is used, but readiness comes from HTTP polling of that port (fetch(probe)). The only ownership check is the `exited` flag, sampled at the top of each loop iteration before the request. It is not raced against the child's exit, and readiness is not taken from the child's own announcement. The port is also released by freePort before the child binds it. A different listener on that port could answer the probe before the child's exit is observed. This matches the guidance's fail pattern.
evidence: scripts/lib/preview.mjs startPreview: `if (exited) throw ...; try { const response = await fetch(probe); if (response.ok) return { port, stop } }` with sleep(150)

votes.rationale: The verifier does reserve an ephemeral port with freePort() and passes --strictPort. But readiness comes from HTTP polling with fetch(probe), not from the child's own announcement of its address. The only ownership check is the `exited` flag, read at the top of each loop iteration before the next fetch. It is not raced against the child's exit. If something else bound the freed port after freePort() closed it, it could answer the probe with a 2xx before the child's failure is observed. The guidance names liveness sampled before each request, plus a strict port, as insufficient. Neither mechanism (a) nor (b) is implemented.

Every rule in how-to.css that targets a kit hook or a generic element sits under `.how-to`. That covers the root, header, title, marker, mode toggle, prev/next buttons, footer, caption, dots, the `[data-presentation-attribution]` hook, the TOC entries, and every rule inside the @media (max-width: 640px) block. Kit hooks used inside the scene are scoped under `.how-to-scene`, the class the presentation puts on its own SceneLayer. Every other selector (.how-to-actor, .how-to-card[data-kind='ghost'], .how-to-arrow path, .how-to-frame-label and so on) is a class namespaced to this presentation. Those classes are its own hooks: only this presentation applies them, in SampleScene.tsx, so the rules cannot match elements in another presentation after client-side navigation. The materialized template presentation.css follows the same pattern. Its kit-hook rules sit under `.__CLASS__`, its other selectors are `.__CLASS__-box` and `.__CLASS__-arrow`, and new-presentation.mjs replaces `__CLASS__` with the slug. Judge C failed the criterion because .how-to-actor, .how-to-card[data-kind='ghost'] and .how-to-arrow path have no `.how-to` ancestor. That reason does not decide the requirement. The requirement allows scoping under the presentation's own root class or hook, and these selectors target the presentation's own namespaced hook classes, which it alone renders. They are not unscoped rules that could leak to other presentations, which is the defect the criterion names. Judges A and B are borne out by the material, so I rule pass.

SceneLayer and the kit's index.ts re-export are not in the packet. SceneLayer is only a layer wrapper and index.ts is only a re-export, so neither affects the proof.

Judges A and C cite the registry-removal and out-of-order e2e faults (tests/e2e/verify.e2e.test.ts:62-75). Those tests are real, but they cover only unregistration and reordering, not absent steps content, which the guidance includes in 'missing sample'. So they do not show that the requirement is met.

After each ArrowRight, a NaN index fails explicitly ('the step hook disappeared') with step i+1. checkAdvance (scripts/lib/verify-core.mjs:94-99) accepts only observed === previous + 1. Errors carry the step and are formatted as 'at step N (index i)' (verify-core.mjs:117-120), and the top-level catch sets exitCode 1 (verify.mjs:168-172). contradiction_checks.rationale: The auditor's claim holds. The review guidance gives a specific fail condition: fail when the transition check turns an absent or non-numeric hook into a number that still passes its comparison, with Number(null) === 0 on the first step as the example. This is a scenario the guidance names, so the general rule against judging hypothetical inputs does not save the pass. That rule also cannot separate the two cases: the candidate never renders an absent hook either, yet the guidance counts both. In scripts/verify.mjs:101, readIndex only maps null/undefined to NaN, using `?? NaN`. An empty or whitespace-only data-step-index is not a number in the plain meaning of "non-numeric". Number('') and Number(' ') are both 0, so on i = 0 the check `if (index !== i)` at line 108 passes, and the verifier treats the bad hook as a valid first step. Later steps are protected by the String(want) wait and checkAdvance, and the step count is protected by `!(count > 0)`. The first-step comparison is still exactly the case the guidance names. The pass's defence is that Presentation.tsx always renders a numeric index. That defence fails because the guidance treats the verifier's handling of these hook values as a requirement on its own, whether or not the candidate ever produces them. The focused render-throw and stalled-transition tests do satisfy the test clause, but meeting one clause does not outweigh an explicit fail condition.

first_results.rationale: The sample presentation owns one stylesheet, how-to.css, which Talk.tsx imports. Talk.tsx wraps the deck in the root class `how-to`. Every rule in how-to.css that targets a kit hook or a generic element sits under `.how-to`. That covers the root, header, title, marker, mode toggle, prev/next buttons, footer, caption, dots, the `[data-presentation-attribution]` hook, the TOC entries, and every rule inside the @media (max-width: 640px) block. Kit hooks used inside the scene are scoped under `.how-to-scene`, the class the presentation puts on its own SceneLayer. Every other selector (.how-to-actor, .how-to-card[data-kind='ghost'], .how-to-arrow path, .how-to-frame-label and so on) is a class namespaced to this presentation. Those classes are its own hooks: only this presentation applies them, in SampleScene.tsx, so the rules cannot match elements in another presentation after client-side navigation. The materialized template presentation.css follows the same pattern. Its kit-hook rules sit under `.__CLASS__`, its other selectors are `.__CLASS__-box` and `.__CLASS__-arrow`, and new-presentation.mjs replaces `__CLASS__` with the slug. Judge C failed the criterion because .how-to-actor, .how-to-card[data-kind='ghost'] and .how-to-arrow path have no `.how-to` ancestor. That reason does not decide the requirement. The requirement allows scoping under the presentation's own root class or hook, and these selectors target the presentation's own namespaced hook classes, which it alone renders. They are not unscoped rules that could leak to other presentations, which is the defect the criterion names. Judges A and B are borne out by the material, so I rule pass.

Kit hooks used inside the scene are scoped under `.how-to-scene`, the class the presentation puts on its own SceneLayer. Every other selector (.how-to-actor, .how-to-card[data-kind='ghost'], .how-to-arrow path, .how-to-frame-label and so on) is a class namespaced to this presentation. Those classes are its own hooks: only this presentation applies them, in SampleScene.tsx, so the rules cannot match elements in another presentation after client-side navigation. The materialized template presentation.css follows the same pattern. Its kit-hook rules sit under `.__CLASS__`, its other selectors are `.__CLASS__-box` and `.__CLASS__-arrow`, and new-presentation.mjs replaces `__CLASS__` with the slug. Judge C failed the criterion because .how-to-actor, .how-to-card[data-kind='ghost'] and .how-to-arrow path have no `.how-to` ancestor. That reason does not decide the requirement. The requirement allows scoping under the presentation's own root class or hook, and these selectors target the presentation's own namespaced hook classes, which it alone renders. They are not unscoped rules that could leak to other presentations, which is the defect the criterion names. Judges A and B are borne out by the material, so I rule pass.

1. Test setup. The integration and end-to-end suites may assume Chromium is already available, from a cache or a prior install. The test plan lists that as setup. This repository's own `npm run verify` may also rely on the `README.md` instruction (`npx playwright install chromium`), because the repository has no hosted CI.

2. The shipped skill. The `README.md` is not part of `skills/presentation/` or the bootstrap, so it cannot serve a generated app. The Playwright npm package is installed by `scaffold.mjs --apply`, but the browser binary is a separate download. A freshly scaffolded app on a machine without Chromium would otherwise fail with a raw launch error. That breaks "does not assume dependencies are installed" and the self-verify gate. The skill must therefore carry an explicit step, in the distributable files, that ensures Chromium before the first render check. The design places this in "the verify step", and `SKILL.md` section 4 (Self-verify) qualifies, as does the scaffold apply step. A suitable form is running `npx playwright install chromium` inside the app directory, which does nothing when the browser is already present. A launch failure in the verify and inspect scripts should also stop with an actionable message that names that command and the failed phase, never a silent skip and never reported as a pass.

Today `SKILL.md` has no such step and the bootstrap carries no setup note, so this is a gap in the distributable skill. It needs a documentation or procedure fix and does not need a new test. The existing test setup and the INT-001 and E2E-001 passes are unaffected.

1. Test setup. The integration and end-to-end suites may assume Chromium is already available, from a cache or a prior install. The test plan lists that as setup. This repository's own `npm run verify` may also rely on the `README.md` instruction (`npx playwright install chromium`), because the repository has no hosted CI.

2. The shipped skill. The `README.md` is not part of `skills/presentation/` or the bootstrap, so it cannot serve a generated app. The Playwright npm package is installed by `scaffold.mjs --apply`, but the browser binary is a separate download. A freshly scaffolded app on a machine without Chromium would otherwise fail with a raw launch error. That breaks "does not assume dependencies are installed" and the self-verify gate. The skill must therefore carry an explicit step, in the distributable files, that ensures Chromium before the first render check. The design places this in "the verify step", and `SKILL.md` section 4 (Self-verify) qualifies, as does the scaffold apply step. A suitable form is running `npx playwright install chromium` inside the app directory, which does nothing when the browser is already present. A launch failure in the verify and inspect scripts should also stop with an actionable message that names that command and the failed phase, never a silent skip and never reported as a pass.

Today `SKILL.md` has no such step and the bootstrap carries no setup note, so this is a gap in the distributable skill. It needs a documentation or procedure fix and does not need a new test. The existing test setup and the INT-001 and E2E-001 passes are unaffected.

In scripts/verify.mjs, readIndex returns Number(getAttribute('data-step-index') ?? NaN). An absent attribute becomes NaN and is rejected, but an existing empty or whitespace-only attribute is not nullish, so Number('') or Number(' ') gives 0. The rendering-exception and stalled-transition tests do not satisfy this separate hook-validation clause, so the pass is defeated.

In all four copies (repository and bootstrap, verify and inspect), every one of those paths reaches a finally block that calls `await preview.stop()`. The judging rules say not to fail on a hypothetical the guidance does not name, so this does not defeat the pass.

engineering-quality.rationale: The auditor read the code correctly. In both direct browser tests in tests/integration/inspect.int.test.ts, startPreview and chromium.launch() are awaited before the try block. If the launch rejects, preview.stop() never runs. But the rubric does not count this against the pass verdict. The guidance for this criterion names two failure cases: a shared hardcoded port, and killing only an npm or npx wrapper while the server keeps running. Browser-launch failure is named only under engineering-preview-terminated-on-every-exit, which covers the scripts, not the tests. The judging rules say a criterion must not fail on a hypothetical scenario its guidance does not name. This guidance also says a hardcoded browser path or a missing browser installation is not scored here. A missing browser is the realistic reason chromium.launch would reject.
